issues.legal_issue: The filing of a suit for dissolution does not, by itself, dissolve a partnership at will or fix the date of its dissolution.
material_facts: A partner filed an earlier suit seeking dissolution, but that suit was dismissed for default and no decree fixing a dissolution date was made.
The present suit treated the filing date of the earlier suit as the date of dissolution.
issues.conclusion: The earlier suit’s filing did not itself dissolve the partnership or fix a dissolution date. A plaint in a dissolution suit is not a notice under section 43; even if service of the summons and plaint were treated as notice, dissolution could take effect only when the last partner was served.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 43(1) and (2) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, a partnership at will is dissolved by written notice to all other partners, effective on the date specified in the notice or, if none is specified, on communication of the notice. A plaint in a suit for dissolution does not satisfy that notice requirement. Under Order 20, rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the court may fix the date of dissolution in a preliminary decree. No earlier case was relied on for this holding.

predicates.partnership_at_will: The partners carried on a partnership that could be dissolved at will.
predicates.dissolution_suit_filed: A partner filed a suit seeking dissolution of the partnership.
predicates.prior_suit_ended_without_decree: The dissolution suit ended without a decree fixing the date of dissolution.

issues.definition: When a partnership at will is the subject of a dissolution suit that ends without a decree, the filing of the suit alone does not dissolve the partnership.

issues.legal_issue: A limitation bar cannot be decided as a pure question of law on appeal when its determination depends on unresolved facts and the affected parties had no fair opportunity to address it.
material_facts: The trial court decreed relief in the suit, but a defendant who had not filed a written statement raised limitation for the first time before the High Court.
Determining the relevant dissolution date could require evidence about when the last partner was served with the summons and plaint.
The record did not establish that service date, and the parties supporting the trial decree had no opportunity to amend their pleadings or present evidence on limitation.
The High Court treated the suit as time-barred and dismissed it.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in treating limitation as a pure question of law and deciding it on appeal without factual inquiry or a fair opportunity for the affected parties to meet the plea. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s decision and restored the trial court’s decree.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 requires a court to take notice of limitation, and Article 106 was invoked in relation to the claim for accounts and profits. But where limitation is a mixed question of fact and law, the court should not decide a newly raised plea without allowing the affected parties to answer it and establishing the necessary facts. The court could have allowed amendment of pleadings, framed an issue, and obtained a finding from the trial court. No earlier case was relied on for this holding.

rule.if: appeal_from_limitation_bar_ruling and limitation_plea_first_raised_on_appeal and limitation_depends_on_unproved_facts and affected_party_denied_opportunity_to_answer

predicates.appeal_from_limitation_bar_ruling: The proceeding is an appeal in which a court has dismissed a claim as time-barred.
predicates.limitation_plea_first_raised_on_appeal: A party first raised the limitation plea at the appellate hearing rather than in the trial pleadings.
predicates.limitation_depends_on_unproved_facts: Deciding whether the claim is late depends on facts that were not established in the record.
predicates.affected_party_denied_opportunity_to_ans: The parties opposing the limitation plea were not given a fair opportunity to amend their pleadings or present evidence in response.

issues.definition: If an appellate limitation ruling rests on a newly raised plea, unresolved facts, and no fair opportunity to respond, the bar cannot stand without factual inquiry and a fair opportunity to answer.
